text:
In late August 1854, cholera struck the crowded Soho district of London, and within days it had become one of the deadliest outbreaks the city had seen. The streets around Broad Street were packed with workshops, tenements and families living several to a room. Sewage ran in open gutters, and many cellars held cesspools that were full to the brim. Within about ten days, roughly five hundred people living within a few hundred yards of one another had died.

Cholera is a violent intestinal illness. It causes sudden, severe diarrhea and vomiting, and the body loses fluid so quickly that a healthy person can be dead within a day or two. In 1854 nobody knew what caused it. The accepted view among most doctors and officials was the miasma theory, which held that disease spread through foul-smelling air rising from rot and filth. Germs had not yet been shown to cause human disease, and the microscope had not yet revealed the tiny organism responsible.

John Snow, a physician who lived and worked nearby, did not accept the miasma idea. He had made his name as a pioneer of anesthesia, and he was known for careful, exact work. During an earlier cholera epidemic in 1848 and 1849 he had noticed something that did not fit the air theory. The illness began with symptoms in the gut, not in the lungs, which suggested to him that people were swallowing something harmful, not breathing it in. He proposed that cholera spread through contaminated water. Few people took the idea seriously.

When the Broad Street outbreak began, Snow saw a chance to test his belief. He went door to door, asking about the sick and the dead. Where had they lived? What had they drunk? He noticed that the deaths clustered tightly around a public water pump on Broad Street, where residents drew their drinking water by hand. People who lived closer to other pumps seemed far less affected.

To make the pattern plain, Snow drew a map. On a street plan of the district he marked each death with a small black bar stacked at the address of the house. The bars piled up around the Broad Street pump like a swarm. The map did not prove anything by itself, but it made the cluster impossible to ignore, and it remains one of the most famous diagrams in the history of public health.

Snow then pursued the exceptions, which convinced him more than the cluster did. Near the pump stood a workhouse housing about five hundred poor residents. Remarkably few of them died. Snow found that the workhouse had its own well and did not rely on the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street also saw no deaths among its workers. The men there were given free beer and mostly drank that, and the brewery also had its own well. Meanwhile, Snow heard of a widow living far away in Hampstead who had died of cholera. Her family told him she had liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle carried to her every day. A niece who had drunk from the same bottle had also fallen ill and died.

By early September, Snow felt he had enough evidence. He took his findings to the local board of guardians, the officials responsible for the parish, and urged them to act. On September 8 they agreed to remove the handle from the Broad Street pump, so that no one could draw water from it. The outbreak was already fading by then, partly because many residents had fled the area, so critics later argued that the handle's removal changed little. Snow himself was cautious about claiming too much for the act.

The story did not end with the pump. Snow kept investigating, and a later inquiry uncovered the likely source. A baby had died of cholera at a house on Broad Street shortly before the outbreak peaked, and the family's waste had drained into a cesspool that was found to be leaking close to the well. The Reverend Henry Whitehead, a local clergyman who began as a skeptic, joined the search. Working with Snow, he traced the first cases and confirmed that the infant's illness preceded the explosion of deaths.

Official opinion was slow to change. A government committee looked into the outbreak and rejected Snow's explanation, sticking to the theory of bad air. Snow died in 1858, still largely unrecognized on the question that mattered most to him. Over the following years, however, the evidence accumulated. London built a modern sewer system, and cholera outbreaks faded. In 1883 the German scientist Robert Koch identified the bacterium that causes cholera, confirming that Snow had been right.

Today Snow is remembered as a founder of epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. His achievement was not a laboratory discovery. He gathered facts, mapped them, hunted for the cases that did not fit, and let the pattern point to a cause long before anyone could see the organism behind it.
